turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Saturday, the twenty-second of August. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three to trade before we start. China jails the man it once made its richest, and quietly closes the Evergrande chapter.
[curious] A coral reef in the living room — and the reefers who'll tell you the tank is the cheapest part of it.
And a little red app that has quietly become the search engine deciding where young Singaporeans eat. That's the weekend.
[warmly] It's a good one. Start me in Shenzhen.
Shenzhen. On Wednesday a court gave Hui Ka Yan life in prison, and confiscated his entire personal fortune.
The Evergrande founder. Once, on paper, the richest person in China.

The same. He pleaded guilty in April — eight charges, fraud, bribery, fraudulent securities issuance. The company was fined eight point eight billion yuan, and more than fifty executives went down with him, two of his own sons among them.
[exhales] Five years after it defaulted on — what was the number?
More than three hundred billion dollars of liabilities. That default was the detonator of the whole property bust.
So is this closure? The end of the story?
[deadpan] It's punctuation, not a plot turn. The company was already liquidated back in twenty twenty-four. Hui had been detained since twenty twenty-three.
Two readings of it in the book, though.
Two. The state media line, from C C T V, is discipline restored — rule of law, reckless borrowing punished according to law.
And the Western read?

Bloomberg and C N N call it a milestone that isn't closure. A scapegoat is sentenced; the deflation underneath is untouched. The buyers still holding contracts for unfinished flats are made whole by exactly none of it.
[thoughtful] And the sceptic in the middle?

That it's theatre. Rhodium's read is that without real stimulus, China's demand growth is nearer two to three per cent — and Beijing keeps declining the property bailout that would actually clear the wreck. Youth unemployment is near seventeen per cent; it's a fourth year of deflationary pressure. Punishing one man performs accountability while the crisis stays wide open.
A tycoon can be sentenced. The debt he built cannot be.
That's the line. Around the desks — Europe spent the week in a furnace. More than twenty-five thousand heat deaths this year, and a national record of forty-one point two degrees in Austria.
[sighs] The shoulder seasons are becoming the season.
On Ukraine, a genuine delta — Washington now thinks the Kremlin might accept a partial air truce. Not a ceasefire. The first shape either side has agreed to discuss in months.
And a number I can't get out of my head.
American gross federal debt crossed forty trillion dollars this week. Hold that one — it's the number under the whole money block.
[curious] Okay, take me there. What is the Fed actually doing?
The opposite of what most people assume. This isn't a story about cuts. It's a story about a possible hike.
Wait — a hike? Really?
They held at three and a half to three and three-quarters per cent in July — but on a nine-to-three vote, with three members dissenting because they wanted to raise rates immediately.
And the new chair is the wildcard.

Kevin Warsh, chair since May. He's thrown out forward guidance and says the Fed will act independently of whatever markets price. So his Jackson Hole speech next Friday, the twenty-eighth, carries unusual weight.
[skeptical] Meanwhile the Treasury is doing its own thing.
This is the week's real move. The thirty-year yield hit a nineteen-year high near five point three four per cent, so the Treasury more than doubled its bond buybacks to prop the long end.
Did it work?
[deadpan] For about a day. The thirty-year dipped, then rebounded and wiped the whole move out. A circuit-breaker, not a cure.
So a Fed that won't ease, a Treasury monetising its own debt, forty trillion in debt behind it —
— and you get the debasement trade. That's why gold sits near four thousand six hundred dollars, and why bitcoin ripped off the low sixty-thousands this week, to around seventy-six thousand.
[curious] Both up at once. That's the tell?

That's the tell. And the honest tension: real rates are high, which historically fights both. So this is a distrust-of-institutions bid, not a cheap-money one. It can unwind fast if Warsh sounds credible on Friday.
Not advice. Explanation.
Never advice on this desk. Home, briefly — tomorrow is the National Day Rally.
[warmly] What's the Prime Minister expected to lead with?
The cost of raising children — infant care, pre-school affordability. Which, for a household with a twelve-year-old, is the interesting gap.
Because the help points at the pre-school gate, not the secondary-school years that are about to get expensive.

Exactly the gap to watch. In the meantime, the cost-of-living payment lands from the ninth of September — four hundred to six hundred dollars — but link your N R I C to PayNow by the thirtieth of August to get it fast.
A calendar note worth keeping. [pause] Right. My favourite kind of story next — the ones you build.
The home lab first. The big open-model event this week was a non-event.
[curious] Meaning?
A Chinese lab, Z-A-I, launched a frontier model called G L M five point three — then declined to release its open weights. Held them back, for a fortnight, over a safety review.
Why?

Because it scored eighty-four and a half per cent on a benchmark for finding software vulnerabilities. It's genuinely good at hacking. A lab pausing its own release because the model is too capable — that's new terrain.
[thoughtful] The open frontier grew a gate.

It did. The useful news for the reader's own machine was quieter — a free tool, Unsloth, shipped better compression, so the model you already run gets faster on the cards you own. The one that actually uses a dual-card rig is still an open model called g-p-t-o-s-s, at around sixty gigabytes — fits, with room to spare.
Which is the whole issue in a sentence, isn't it. You don't always need a bigger card. You need a better-run one.
[warmly] That's the spine. Same as the reef-keeper's better skimmer.
And in The Kit — Sennheiser did something small and quietly radical.
New flagship earbuds, the Momentum True Wireless Five, at two hundred and ninety-nine dollars ninety-five. The one feature that matters: the batteries, in the buds and the case, are user-replaceable.
[excited] So it doesn't just die in two years and take the whole thing with it.
That's the argument. A three-hundred-dollar object designed to outlive its own battery. The catch — the noise cancelling still has to catch Bose and Sony, and that's unproven.
Buy it for the sound and the repairability, not the promise on the box.
And then there's the Atelier. This week: claw machines.
[laughs] The claw machine? The one everybody says is rigged?
Both halves of that sentence are true, and that's the whole piece. The cabinet is simple. The money hides in one setting.
Go on.
Western machines run a payout model — the claw is given full grip only about one play in eighteen. It's a slot machine wearing a crane costume.
[skeptical] And the Japanese ones?
The U F O Catcher lineage is tuned for skill — a bridge setting where a genuinely better player wins more. But even there, fairness is a setting, not a property.
So why on earth own one?
[wry] Because when you own it, the dip switches are yours. Set it to full grip and free play, and it stops being a slot in costume and becomes what it always looked like — a skill toy.
The one claw machine you can trust is the one whose settings you control. I love that.
Singapore drew its own line, by the way — capped the prize value at a hundred dollars and banned cash payouts back in twenty twenty-four.
[amused] Regulating the claw machine. Only here. [pause] Okay. Take my hand.
[sighs] Here we go.
We're going down the rabbit hole.
[deadpan] Every morning with this one.
[laughs] Reef aquariums! Talk to me. What is it, really?
It's not keeping fish. It's running a slice of the tropical ocean inside three narrow numbers — temperature, salinity, and the one they obsess over, alkalinity, which the corals eat as they grow.
The corals are the point.
The fish are garnish. And the community's own shorthand for the whole thing is merciless — the tank is the cheapest part.
[chuckles] Of course it is. Where does the money actually go?
Everywhere. A prestige light is around nine hundred dollars. A grail skimmer, from a German maker, about eighteen hundred — buy it once, will it to your children.
And I've heard there's a pump —

[excited] The Abyzz. A return pump that costs about two thousand eight hundred dollars. There's a recurring forum thread whose entire title is just, what is the buzz about a two-thousand-eight-hundred-dollar pump.
And they buy it anyway.
They buy it anyway. And the corals themselves are a collectible economy — a single branded mushroom, an O-G Bounce, lists at five hundred and ninety-nine dollars, and has held its value for a decade.
[gasps] Six hundred dollars for one mushroom.
For one mushroom. Now — the honesty. There's a phrase, the reef tax.
Which is?
The losses. Everything in the box is alive, and alive things die. A single heater failure or a dosing slip can wipe out years of work overnight. Tank-crash threads are their own genre.
[thoughtful] So what does the community itself admit when you press it?

The quiet part. That abandoned tanks are common — and that the ocean does not need a ten-thousand-dollar box in your living room. Marketing sells serenity; the reality is a demanding live system with real casualties.
And the Singapore twist? There's always one.

The chiller. In a thirty-degree flat the tank heats itself through its own pumps and lights, so you need a chiller — a few hundred dollars, plus the electricity. It's the buy-once cost every glossy guide skips.
[warmly] A miniature ocean, and a running bill to keep it cold. That's the descent.
That's the descent. Come up for air — culture and the body.
The family option at the cinema?

Enid Blyton's Magic Faraway Tree finally reaches American screens — Andrew Garfield, Claire Foy. Its actual theme is unplugging, which for a house negotiating a twelve-year-old's screen time is either on the nose or well timed.
[chuckles] And the record?
Weezer's twentieth album, the Gold Album, swinging one more time for the sound they made when this reader was in his twenties. Early scores are warm but on a thin sample — treat it as provisional.
Speaking of the body — you said something about Zone Two earlier that I didn't like.

[wry] I did. A twenty twenty-five review titled, and I'm quoting, Much Ado About Zone Two. The finding: when volume's matched, the easy pace is not uniquely magic. Higher intensity does as much or more.
So the longevity crowd's favourite pace —

— is base, not magic. Protect one weekly hard session, because the number that actually tracks how long you live is your V-O-two max. Climb from the bottom fitness quarter to merely average, and it's associated with about half the mortality.
[thoughtful] Half. And the family desk?
The first real data on Australia's under-sixteen social media ban is in. More than eighty-five per cent of kids kept using the platforms anyway.
So it didn't work?
Here's the uncomfortable part — it worked least on the youngest kids. Daily use among twelve and thirteen-year-olds stayed flat. The wall moved the needle least exactly where it was aimed hardest.
A wall, and a twelve-year-old is a climber.
And a lovely companion finding — her late bedtime isn't defiance, it's chemistry. Puberty pushes melatonin back by about two hours. The fix is morning light, not an earlier curfew she can't obey.
[warmly] That one's a gift to a lot of parents. Anything to actually book?

The easy win needs no ticket — the Singapore Night Festival is free and on right now, through the fifth of September. And a new one for the food desk: a tonkatsu counter built entirely on ten-day dry-aged Jeju pork, in the C B D.
[amused] Dry-aged pork cutlet. Now you're talking. And it's a weekend, so — travel.
The Grand Tour is Ishigaki and the Yaeyama islands. Subtropical Japan at the bottom of the map — turquoise reef, and the country's first dark-sky park.
[excited] Reef and stars. That's the dream. What's the catch?
Two catches, honestly told. The famous turquoise lagoon, Kabira Bay — you can't swim in it. It's a black-pearl cultivation site. You ride a glass-bottom boat and look.
[laughs] Of course you can't swim in the pretty one. And the stars?

You can see the Southern Cross from there — but only from about late December to mid-June. An autumn traveller gets a spectacular Milky Way, not the Cross. Don't promise yourself the Cross in October.
But you can swim with the mantas.
You can — a cleaning station off the coast, roughly April to November. The trap is that peak manta season is also peak typhoon season. The postcard and the risk share a calendar.
[thoughtful] And the weak yen makes the whole thing —
— merely expensive instead of extravagant. About a hundred and twenty-four yen to the Singapore dollar. The exchange rate does real work.
[warmly] Alright. Bring us down for the last one. Slower.
[pause] The Undercurrent. Picture a Saturday in Bangsar, or on Orchard Road. A twenty-four-year-old wants lunch.
And she doesn't open Google.
She opens a red app — Xiaohongshu, the Little Red Book — and she searches, in Chinese, for a café. She reads three write-ups by people who actually went, and orders the exact dish in the photo.
So it's not a feed anymore. It's a search engine.

It's the search of record. And that's the whole point — whoever owns that moment, the point of decision, owns default reality. In Malaysia it's now the second-largest market outside China. In Singapore, projected to reach a quarter of the population by year's end.
[thoughtful] And her Malay and Indian classmates?
Are on TikTok and Instagram, in a different aesthetic universe. Same city. A different internet.
That's the unsettling part, isn't it. Not that the app is Chinese.

It's that adoption tracks language. One cohort increasingly lives inside a China-shaped world — moderated under Chinese content law, censored on exactly what Beijing censors — while their neighbours live in the American-platform one.
[exhales] Two feeds, one city, splitting along mother tongue.

And it arrives in the friendliest possible disguise. A red icon that only ever wanted to show you a nicer café — and, two doors down, the Chinese ice-cream chain and the toy shop it surfaced, paid for in four easy instalments. When the Financial Times writes it up, it'll be about market share. The actual stakes are a shared public quietly coming apart.
[drawn out] We make the tool. And thereafter the tool makes us.
[warmly] Culkin's line. The whole issue in nine words. Build the tool carefully — it's building you.
[pause] That's a place to stop.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
